highlights.quote: The bone does not contain the direction of intention. It contains the direction of force.
highlights.judgment: Compact, genuinely earned formulation of the book's central epistemic caution about physical evidence.

highlights.quote: No marching army is required for coercion to begin. The ration list already distinguishes those who issue from those who receive.
highlights.judgment: The thesis stated at its strongest — administration as the origin, not the servant, of organized force.

highlights.quote: The house establishes proximity; it does not establish motive.
highlights.judgment: Excellent discipline in separating what a trace preserves from what interpretation adds.

highlights.quote: In 1789, John James Audubon painted the famous image often called *The Zong Massacre*
highlights.judgment: A conspicuous fabricated attribution (Audubon was four years old; the painting is Turner's), and the sentence then contradicts itself — the worst evidentiary lapse in the book.

highlights.quote: The Dar al-Hadith al-Nuriyya in Damascus, founded in 1172 after Nur al-Din’s death had already occurred
highlights.judgment: Internally incoherent: the chapter dates that death to 1174, so the clause is both wrong and self-defeating.

highlights.quote: Prison authorities communicated with municipal officials, and some did.
highlights.judgment: A broken, truncated sentence that survived to the final draft — evidence of unfinished line-editing.

highlights.quote: The Germans knew only that the rising had spread faster than their patrols, without knowing how many people followed him.
highlights.judgment: Dangling pronoun with no antecedent in the sentence; a recurring symptom of clause-reordering left unchecked.

highlights.quote: Machinery enlarged the hand, but political authority chose where it would close.
highlights.judgment: Vivid and apt, but typical of the aphoristic chapter-closer the book reaches for almost every time.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Nearly every chapter opens with a dramatised, novelistic set-piece (weather, gestures, invented dialogue) before pivoting to analysis — a template so regular that the reader learns to wait out the scene.
instances: The four men stood beneath the painted beams of the chapter house at Canterbury on 30 December 1170
The stone was wet when Narmer’s men carried it into the open court at Nekhen.

recurringPatterns.pattern: A standardised comparative pivot that dismisses a strawman contrast in identical syntax before restating the institutional thesis.
instances: Neither case fits the picture of nomads who only raided and moved on.
Neither case fits the picture of an enraged population suddenly losing control.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Isolated one-sentence paragraphs used as rhetorical punctuation between analytic blocks, at a rate of several per chapter.
instances: A population appears as the object of a command.
The religious reputation had to survive contact with administration.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Semicolon or comma antithesis of the form 'X did one thing; it did not do the other', deployed as the default way to end an argumentative paragraph.
instances: The house establishes proximity; it does not establish motive.
A wampum belt recorded a relation; it did not register a tax.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Chapter and book endings resolve into an aphoristic summary clause naming offices, traces or choices, so that closure always sounds the same note.
instances: the history of aggression becomes a record of choices about who could be harmed, by whom, and under whose protection.
The future will still turn on decisions made by people at desks, in meeting rooms, at checkpoints, and before crowds.

summary: This is a serious, unusually coherent work of comparative history whose thesis — that aggression becomes historically consequential only when an office classifies a population, authorises harm, and supplies the means — is stated in chapter 1 and genuinely tested, rather than merely restated, across fifteen chapters spanning Çatalhöyük to Colombia. Its greatest strength is evidentiary discipline: it repeatedly distinguishes what a skull, a chronicle, a relief or a protocol can establish from what interpretation adds, and it stages real interpretive disagreements (Jebel Sahaba, Erlitou's earthworks, the September Massacres' spontaneity) without collapsing them into a verdict. The prose is clean, concrete, and rarely abstract, with sustained control of a cool, forensic register. The costs are structural repetition and a few lapses that should not have survived: every chapter runs the same dramatised-scene-then-analysis machine, the comparative pivots and one-sentence rhetorical beats recur to the point of predictability, and the closing aphorism is a fixed habit. Two factual failures matter — an invented Audubon attribution for the Zong image, and a Dar al-Hadith founding date that contradicts the chapter's own account of Nur al-Din's death — alongside at least one broken sentence and a dangling pronoun. With a line-edit for those errors and a deliberate variation of the chapter template, this would be ready.
